Description: A mild viral infection of the nose and throat. Usually settles on its own within 7-10 days. Antibiotics do not help because the cause is a virus.
Medicines_Educational: Paracetamol (fever/pain); Cetirizine (runny nose); Saline nasal drops; Steam inhalation. Antibiotics are NOT useful for a viral cold.
Home_Care: Warm fluids, adequate sleep, steam inhalation, avoid cold drinks.
Common_Symptoms: Sneezing; Runny nose; Sore throat; Mild cough; Mild fever; Headache
Causes: More than 200 viruses, most often rhinovirus. Spreads through droplets from coughs and sneezes, or by touching contaminated surfaces and then the face.
Precautions: See a doctor if symptoms last more than 10 days, or if there is high fever or ear pain.

Description: A viral infection with sudden high fever, body ache and chills. Spreads easily, so rest and isolation help. Annual vaccination reduces risk.
Medicines_Educational: Paracetamol; Oseltamivir (only if a doctor prescribes it early); Cetirizine for sneezing. Bed rest and plenty of fluids.
Home_Care: Bed rest, warm soups, isolate from family members, use a mask.
Common_Symptoms: Sudden high fever; Body and muscle ache; Dry cough; Headache; Chills; Tiredness
Causes: Influenza A and B viruses. Spreads mainly through airborne droplets. New strains appear every year, which is why the vaccine is repeated annually.
Precautions: Seek help if breathing becomes difficult, or if fever lasts beyond 5 days.

Description: A nonspecific fever caused by a viral infection. The fever usually lasts 3-5 days and improves with rest, fluids and fever control.
Medicines_Educational: Paracetamol for fever and body ache; Oral rehydration salts; Sponging with lukewarm water for high fever.
Home_Care: Plenty of water and ORS, light easily digestible food, complete rest.
Common_Symptoms: Fever; Headache; Body pain; Tiredness; Loss of appetite; Nausea
Causes: A group of common viral infections rather than one specific virus. Spreads through droplets or contaminated food and water.
Precautions: See a doctor if fever crosses 103 F, lasts more than 3 days, or if there is a rash or bleeding.

Description: A mosquito-borne viral infection. Fever is often very high and is accompanied by severe joint and muscle pain and sometimes a skin rash. Some cases become severe, so monitoring platelet counts is important.
Medicines_Educational: Paracetamol for fever and pain. AVOID aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers (NSAIDs) unless a doctor approves them, because of bleeding risk. Hospital monitoring if warning signs appear.
Home_Care: Strict bed rest, 3-4 litres of fluids per day, monitor temperature every 4-6 hours, watch for bleeding gums or nose bleeds.
Common_Symptoms: Very high fever; Severe joint and muscle pain; Skin rash; Headache; Nausea; Pain behind the eyes
Causes: Dengue virus, spread by the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. These mosquitoes breed in clean stagnant water and usually bite during the day.
Precautions: GO TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY if there is severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums, black stools or cold clammy skin.

Description: A mosquito-borne parasitic infection. It characteristically causes recurring high fever with severe chills. It needs a blood test for confirmation and specific treatment.
Medicines_Educational: Antimalarial drugs (e.g. chloroquine/artemisinin combination therapy) prescribed by a doctor after a positive blood test; Paracetamol for fever.
Home_Care: Complete rest, high fluid intake, use a mosquito net, take medicines at fixed times.
Common_Symptoms: High fever with shivering chills; Headache; Vomiting; Tiredness; Heavy sweating
Causes: Plasmodium parasites, spread by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, which bites mainly between dusk and dawn.
Precautions: Get a blood test immediately; do not self-medicate; return if vomiting prevents you from taking fluids.

Description: A bacterial infection of the gut spread through contaminated food or water. It causes a long, stepwise rising fever along with abdominal symptoms.
Medicines_Educational: A full course of antibiotics (e.g. azithromycin, cefixime) as prescribed by a doctor. Never stop a course midway.
Home_Care: Soft, bland, low-fibre food; boiled or bottled water; complete rest.
Common_Symptoms: Fever that rises step by step over days; Stomach pain; Headache; Constipation or loose motions; Weakness; Loss of appetite
Causes: Salmonella typhi bacteria, spread through food or water contaminated by the faeces of an infected person.
Precautions: See a doctor for a blood culture test; untreated typhoid can cause intestinal perforation.

Description: A lung infection in which the air sacs fill with fluid. It causes a productive cough and difficulty in breathing, and needs prompt medical treatment.
Medicines_Educational: Antibiotics as prescribed; Paracetamol for fever; Nebulisation or oxygen if breathing is difficult. This usually needs hospital care.
Home_Care: Rest in a semi-sitting position, warm fluids, follow up urgently if breathing worsens.
Common_Symptoms: Cough with phlegm; Difficulty in breathing; Fever with chills; Chest pain; Tiredness
Causes: Bacteria (most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses or fungi infect the air sacs of the lungs, which then fill with fluid.
Precautions: MEDICAL EMERGENCY if lips turn blue, breathing is very fast, or there is confusion. Go to hospital now.

Description: A long-term inflammatory condition of the airways. Symptoms come in episodes triggered by dust, pollen, cold air or exercise. Inhalers are the mainstay of control.
Medicines_Educational: Salbutamol inhaler for sudden attacks; Inhaled corticosteroid (e.g. budesonide) for long-term control; Montelukast. Inhalers are safe and not habit-forming.
Home_Care: Avoid dust, smoke and cold air; keep the inhaler with you at all times; do breathing exercises.
Common_Symptoms: Episodes of difficulty in breathing; Wheezing; Dry cough, worse at night; Chest tightness
Causes: Long-term inflammation of the airways with a genetic tendency. Attacks are triggered by dust, pollen, cold air, smoke or exercise. It is not infectious.
Precautions: Go to hospital if the inhaler does not relieve an attack within 15 minutes.

Description: A bacterial infection that mainly affects the lungs and spreads through the air. It requires a long course of treatment and is a public-health priority case.
Medicines_Educational: A fixed combination of anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) taken daily for 6 months or more, free of cost at government DOTS centres.
Home_Care: High-protein, high-calorie diet; cover the mouth while coughing; ventilate the room; never skip doses.
Common_Symptoms: Cough lasting more than 2 weeks; Blood in sputum; Night sweats; Weight loss; Evening fever; Tiredness
Causes: Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria, spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Spreads fastest in crowded, poorly ventilated places.
Precautions: Do not share food or utensils; complete the entire course; report weight loss or blood in sputum.

Description: Inflammation of the stomach and intestines, usually from an infection. The main risk is dehydration, so fluids and salts matter most.
Medicines_Educational: Oral rehydration salts (ORS); Zinc supplements; Antibiotics only if a bacterial cause is confirmed. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medicines without medical advice.
Home_Care: ORS after every loose motion, bland food such as rice and curd, avoid oily and spicy food.
Common_Symptoms: Loose motions; Vomiting; Stomach cramps; Nausea; Mild fever
Causes: Viruses (such as rotavirus and norovirus), bacteria or parasites, spread through contaminated food, water or hands.
Precautions: See a doctor if there is blood in the stools, no urine for 8 hours, or signs of severe dehydration.

Description: Illness caused by eating food contaminated with bacteria or their toxins. It starts within hours of the meal, with vomiting and loose motions.
Medicines_Educational: Oral rehydration salts; Plenty of fluids; Paracetamol if there is fever. Vomiting usually settles in 24-48 hours.
Home_Care: Stop eating solid food for a few hours, sip ORS slowly and frequently.
Common_Symptoms: Vomiting starting within hours of eating; Loose motions; Stomach cramps; Nausea; Dizziness
Causes: Toxins or bacteria (Staphylococcus, Salmonella, E. coli) in food that was stale, undercooked or left unrefrigerated.
Precautions: See a doctor if symptoms last more than 2 days or there is blood in vomit or stools.

Description: A recurring type of headache, often one-sided and throbbing, sometimes with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Triggers vary from person to person.
Medicines_Educational: Paracetamol or a doctor-prescribed painkiller; An anti-emetic (e.g. domperidone) for nausea; Rest in a dark, quiet room.
Home_Care: Rest in a dark quiet room, cold compress on the forehead, note down what triggered the attack.
Common_Symptoms: One-sided throbbing headache; Nausea; Vomiting; Sensitivity to light and sound; Blurred vision
Causes: A neurological condition with a genetic tendency. Attacks are triggered by stress, lack of sleep, skipped meals, strong smells or certain foods. It is NOT caused by a brain tumour.
Precautions: See a doctor if the headache is sudden and severe, or comes with weakness or slurred speech.

Description: Persistently raised blood pressure. It usually has no symptoms for years but silently damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes.
Medicines_Educational: Blood-pressure medicines are lifelong and must only be started or changed by a doctor, e.g. amlodipine, telmisartan, hydrochlorothiazide. Lifestyle changes reduce the dose needed.
Home_Care: Reduce salt, walk 30 minutes daily, stop smoking, reduce weight, check BP twice a week.
Common_Symptoms: Usually no symptoms at all; Headache; Dizziness; Palpitations; Blurred vision
Causes: Persistently raised blood pressure. Contributing causes include excess salt, obesity, lack of exercise, stress, alcohol and heredity. In most patients no single cause is found.
Precautions: See a doctor immediately for chest pain, breathlessness, or a very severe headache. Do not stop medicines on your own.

Description: A long-term condition in which blood sugar stays high because the body does not make or properly use insulin. Needs lifelong lifestyle care and monitoring.
Medicines_Educational: Metformin is the usual first medicine; Insulin for some patients. Diet, exercise and regular blood-sugar testing are as important as tablets.
Home_Care: Sugar-free diet, daily exercise, regular foot care, monitor blood sugar as advised.
Common_Symptoms: Frequent urination; Excessive thirst; Tiredness; Weight loss; Blurred vision; Slow-healing wounds
Causes: The body either does not make enough insulin (type 1) or cannot use it properly (type 2). Type 2 is strongly linked to obesity, inactivity and family history.
Precautions: See a doctor urgently if there is confusion, very high sugar, deep rapid breathing or a non-healing wound.

Description: An allergic reaction of the nose and eyes to dust, pollen or animal hair. It is not infectious and often runs in families.
Medicines_Educational: Non-sedating antihistamines (e.g. loratadine, cetirizine); Saline nasal rinse; Steroid nasal spray for persistent symptoms.
Home_Care: Keep the house dust-free, wash bedding in hot water, avoid pets during peak season.
Common_Symptoms: Frequent sneezing; Runny nose; Itchy watery eyes; Blocked nose; Skin rash
Causes: An allergic reaction to dust mites, pollen, animal hair or mould. It is not an infection and does not spread from person to person.
Precautions: See a doctor if there is wheezing or breathlessness.

Description: An infection of the bladder or urinary tract, commonly caused by bacteria entering from outside. Very common in women.
Medicines_Educational: Antibiotics as prescribed; Paracetamol for fever and pain; Drink 2-3 litres of water a day.
Home_Care: Drink plenty of water, do not hold urine, maintain personal hygiene.
Common_Symptoms: Burning while passing urine; Frequent urge to urinate; Lower abdominal pain; Fever; Cloudy or foul-smelling urine
Causes: Bacteria, usually E. coli, entering the urinary tract. More common in women because the urethra is shorter. Holding urine and poor hygiene raise the risk.
Precautions: See a doctor if there is back pain with high fever, or blood in the urine. Men with these symptoms need prompt review.

Description: A shortage of healthy red blood cells or haemoglobin. The commonest cause in India is iron deficiency. It causes tiredness and breathlessness.
Medicines_Educational: Iron and folic acid tablets (usually taken with vitamin C); Vitamin B12 if deficient. Always confirm the type of anaemia with a blood test first.
Home_Care: Iron-rich food: green leafy vegetables, dates, jaggery, liver; avoid tea or coffee with meals.
Common_Symptoms: Tiredness; Dizziness; Shortness of breath; Pale skin; Palpitations; Headache
Causes: Too little haemoglobin or too few red blood cells. In India the commonest cause is iron deficiency; others are vitamin B12 deficiency, blood loss and long-term disease.
Precautions: See a doctor if there is chest pain, breathlessness at rest, or fainting.

Description: Inflammation of the liver, most often caused by a virus. The liver may not work normally, which shows up as yellow eyes and skin.
Medicines_Educational: Rest; A high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet; Vitamin supplements. Hepatitis A and E usually recover with supportive care; B and C need specialist treatment.
Home_Care: Complete rest, no alcohol at all, low-fat food, drink boiled water.
Common_Symptoms: Yellow eyes and skin; Loss of appetite; Nausea and vomiting; Tiredness; Dark urine; Stomach pain
Causes: Usually a viral infection (hepatitis A, B, C, D or E). A and E spread through contaminated food and water; B and C spread through infected blood, needles and unprotected sex. Alcohol and some drugs also damage the liver.
Precautions: See a doctor urgently if drowsiness, confusion or bleeding develops. Avoid alcohol and self-medication completely.
